newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Cuba blasts U.S. at Earth Summit.
newsitem.headline: Cuba blasts U.S. at Earth Summit.

text.p: Cuba launched a fierce attack against the United States at the U.N. Earth Summit on Tuesday, saying "capitalist greed" was the main cause environmental damage threatening mankind's survival.
The speaker of Cuba's parliament, Ricardo Alarcon, said his country had a particularly hard time because of the "economic, political and even biological war unleashed...by the United States."

This referred to a Cuban charge, first made in May and denied by Washington, that the United States had committed "biological aggression" by spraying plant-destroying insects from a crop-dusting plane over western Cuba.

"Capitalist greed is the principal cause of the unjust world and of the severe damage to nature which is threatening the survival of humankind today. It is absurd to try to cure those evils with blind worship of market, with more selfishness, with more capitalism," said Alarcon, a former foreign minister.
Alarcon said that sustainable development was a hard goal for the Third World and "for Cuba it proves even harder."
He said that five years after the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, environmental problems had worsened.
The second Earth Summit at the United Nations this week, attended by 173 nations, is taking stock of progress and failures since the Rio meeting.

In a news conference near the United Nations, the estranged daughter of Cuban leader Fidel Castro accused the Havana government of widespread environmental abuses and pollution that had damaged the health of the population.

"Erosion and pollution is not only affecting the ecosystems in our country but people as well," Alina Fernandez Revuelta told the news conference sponsored by the "Coalition for a Free and Green Cuba."
Fernandez, who left Cuba in 1994, said her father did not care about pollution, and persecuted environmental activists.

The Coalition had documented 450 cases of alleged environmental abuse, including the destruction of coral reefs, desertification and the pollution of waterways, according to another member of the coalition, Andres Solares.
The country faced a widespread shortage of water, and salinization had made tracts of agricultural land unusable, Solares said.
